docs.title: 長時間學習不能保證你得好成績 How to Get a High GPA Without Making University All About Studying
docs.text:
One of the biggest misconceptions about university is that a high GPA requires constant studying.

While academic performance matters for opportunities such as scholarships, exchange programmes, and postgraduate study, strong grades are often the result of effective planning and smart decision-making rather than endless hours of revision. The following five habits can help.

docs.title: 1. Study the Assessment Before the Content
docs.text:
Before diving into lecture slides, review the assessment breakdown and marking rubric.

Understanding how a course is assessed helps you prioritise your effort. Some students spend hours preparing for examinations while overlooking coursework, participation, or presentations that could provide valuable marks.

The rubric is equally important. Rather than focusing only on completing an assignment, focus on what the rubric rewards. It often provides the clearest indication of what distinguishes a satisfactory submission from an excellent one.

docs.title: 2.Practise Questions Early
docs.text:
Many students wait until revision week before attempting past-paper questions. By then, it is often too late to identify and address weaknesses effectively.

Instead, start practising throughout the semester. A useful target is to complete at least one past-paper question for each course every week.

Regular practice helps identify weaknesses early, develop familiarity with examination-style questions, and build confidence well before the examination period begins.

Students can also make use of the (Library Examination Database)[https://www.library.ln.edu.hk/en/collection/digital/examdb].

docs.title: 3. Stay Ahead of Deadlines
docs.text:
One of the biggest challenges in university is managing multiple deadlines at the same time.

At the beginning of each semester, record all assignments, presentations, projects, quizzes, and examinations in a planner or Gantt chart. This helps identify busy periods early and avoid last-minute surprises.

Starting work ahead of time also creates opportunities to seek feedback, clarify uncertainties, and improve the quality of your work. Many students lose marks not because they lack ability, but because they begin too late.

docs.title: 4. Start Group Projects Early
docs.text:
Group projects often become stressful because planning starts too late.

As soon as groups are formed, establish a communication channel, agree on responsibilities, and set internal deadlines before the official submission date. Regular check-ins can help identify problems before they become serious.

Successful group projects are usually the result of clear expectations, early coordination, and consistent communication.

docs.title: 5. Use AI for Feedback
docs.text:
AI can be a valuable learning tool when used appropriately.

After completing a draft yourself, use AI to identify weaknesses, suggest improvements, or provide examples of stronger responses. Comparing your work with stronger examples can reveal areas for improvement and help you produce higher-quality submissions.

However, AI should be treated as a source of feedback rather than an authority. Lecturers, not AI, determine your grades, so assessment criteria and course requirements should always take priority.

Final Thoughts

A high GPA is not simply the result of studying longer hours. It is often the result of understanding how courses are assessed, preparing consistently, managing deadlines effectively, and seeking feedback early.

By working strategically rather than endlessly, you can achieve strong academic results while still making time for the experiences that make university memorable. A high GPA should be a by-product of working efficiently, not a result of sacrificing everything else university has to offer.

Author: Ed

docs.title: 簡單的選科指南 Simple Guide to Course Registration
docs.text: Course Registration is the key process that determines your schedule for the upcoming semester. With careful planning, it is possible to achieve your ideal schedule, such as having no classes for a full day or avoiding 9:00 AM classes. Please follow these four steps to complete your preparations:

docs.title: First Step: Study Plan
docs.text:
Please log in to the Degree Works system to set up your annual study plan. For detailed instructions on how to use the system, please refer to the Official Guide provided by the university.

  • Basic Requirements: You simply need to add five courses per semester that meet graduation requirements.
  • Course Strategy:
    • Foundation Courses: It is recommended that freshmen prioritize core required courses such as "Common Core," "Chinese Communication," and "University English," as these have clear structures suitable for the transition period.
    • Major Courses: Major courses are typically more challenging; it is advised to progress gradually and avoid rushing into them at the start of your studies.
    • Free Electives: Free electives should be chosen based on personal interest or career planning. You may also use these to fulfill requirements for a Minor.
  • Prerequisites: Some advanced courses have "Prerequisites." Specific requirements are listed on the Student Portfolio page. The system will reject saving your plan if it conflicts with these prerequisites or the term in which the course is offered (if only available in a single semester).
  • Course Load Limit: While the system allows you to register for up to six courses per semester, please consider the academic pressure. Unless you need to retake failed courses or pursue a Minor, it is advised not to challenge the six-course limit to avoid a heavy workload that could affect your learning quality.

docs.title: Second step: Academic Advising
docs.text:
Once you have drafted your plan, it must be approved by your Academic Adviser.

  1. Locate your Adviser: You can find the name of your assigned Academic Adviser on the "Plan" page in Degree Works.
  2. Request Approval: Please send an email to your Adviser to request approval for your annual study plan. Once you have received their consent, you may proceed to the next stage of registration.
    • Tip: Log in to your Outlook school email; when you type your Adviser's name in the "To" field, the system will automatically pop up their email address.

docs.title: Third step：Registration Period
docs.text:
After completing the procedures above, the university will randomly assign class schedules based on your selected courses, which you can view once the Registration Period begins. You can view in via myLingnan Portal, please refer to the Official Guide for detail.

  • Schedule Adjustment: During the registration period, you can adjust your class times according to your personal preferences. Please note that adjustments are not guaranteed: you can only switch into a section if there is still a vacancy (Quota).
  • Course Swapping: You may also change your courses during this time, provided there is still capacity and the course fulfills graduation requirements.
  • Important Dates: The specific dates for the Registration Period will be notified via email before the start of the academic year, and each period lasts for about one day. Please be sure to operate on time:
    • Freshmen: 18th August 2026 , 10:00 – 23:59
    • Senior Year Students: 19th August, 2026, 10:00 – 23:59

Note: Since quotas for popular courses and preferred time slots are limited, it is recommended to log in and confirm or adjust your schedule as soon as the registration opens.

docs.title: Final Step: Add-drop Period
docs.text:
After the semester officially begins, there will be an "Add-drop Period" lasting about one week. You can still adjust your schedule and change courses during this time.

  • Operational Strategy: Since most vacancies for popular courses will have been filled, the success rate for switching is relatively low; therefore, it is not recommended to make major changes to your course selection during this period.
  • Exceptions: If you find that the teaching content or style does not meet your expectations, or if you find the course content overwhelming after classes begin, you may use this period for necessary adjustments.

docs.title: The Limitations of AI: It Cannot Replace Your Unique Insights
docs.text:
One of the biggest flaw of AI in academic life is its lack of genuine human experience and deep insight. When I once asked Gemini to suggest topics for my next article in this Guidebook, its responses were quite generic:

  • A Guide to Freshman Adjustment: Exploring ways to cope with new learning environments, dormitory life, and social pressures.
  • Campus Life Hacks: Sharing practical tips to improve efficiency in daily university life.
  • Scholarship and Financial Planning: Organizing information on government assistance schemes (Grant/Loan) and institutional scholarships.

While these suggestions are correct, they lack a "human soul." Gemini has never spent a single day taking classes at Lingnan University; it cannot understand how AI policies truly affect a student's studies and mindset. Precisely because it lacks this empathetic perspective, it could never produce content with this level of practical warning experience.

This is why you must cherish your own perspective—your critical thinking, your observations, and the personal insights you have forged from your real-life campus experience are values that AI can neither imitate nor replace.

By: Daniel

docs.title: 社交，不在成績表上的必修科 Socializing, the Unofficial Course
docs.text:
Navigating the social landscape of university is the first major challenge every freshman must overcome.

Unlike the static, often insular environment of high school, university life is defined by its fluidity. You will rarely meet the same person in two different classes, and once a semester ends, connections often fade away. Therefore, you must seize every opportunity to connect, take the initiative, and never be afraid to show your true self.

To expand your social circle, the key is active participation:

  • Orientation Events: These are the prime opportunities to make a strong first impression.
  • Student Societies: These are gold mines for finding like-minded peers. (You can find a list of student societies and their contact information in contacts list.)
  • Joining Executive Committees (Cabinets): If you crave the experience of working shoulder-to-shoulder with others to achieve something greater, this is the most immersive path.
  • Hostel Life: This is one of the few settings where you can build stable, long-term relationships. Be sure to foster a good rapport with your neighbors.

As you enter university, you may notice that social interactions sometimes carry an element of "transactional value." Active students often find themselves in high demand for group projects; upperclassmen are frequently sought after for academic advice; and when it comes to competitions or startups, people naturally turn to their networks to find partners. This does not mean university social life is inherently mercenary; it is simply the nature of the environment. Yet, rest assured that genuine, platonic friendship will never be absent in university. As long as you offer companionship, care, and sincerity, those warm connections will never be forgotten.

The good news is that university offers the widest exposure to different people you will likely encounter in your life. In high school, you may have felt pressured to suppress your true self just to "fit in." In the workplace, your social circle is often limited by departmental roles. But in university, every class introduces you to hundreds of new faces, and each semester brings a fresh start.

There is a unique breadth and diversity here that allows you to find your true tribe. Please feel free to express your authentic self—there is no need to dim your light just to accommodate others.

I hope that in this "compulsory course" of social life, you not only learn how to build meaningful connections but also find the answers you are looking for.

By: Daniel

docs.title: 不要像我一延畢 Don't get dalyed in graduation like me
docs.text:
"Graduation requirements" might sound like something you only need to worry about during your senior year—after all, four years is a long time. However, at Lingnan University, some of these requirements must be accumulated starting from your very first year. You won’t officially cross the finish line until they are fully completed right before graduation!

To avoid facing delayed graduation (like I did), make sure to save this list and start planning your university life early.

docs.title: Lingnan University Graduation Requirements at a Glance
docs.text:
To graduate from the university, you must fulfill five major requirements, covering both academic performance and co-curricular development:

  1. cGPA Requirement
  2. ILP (Integrated Learning Programme) Hours
  3. English Language Graduation Requirements (ELGR)
  4. Service Learning (SL)
  5. Information Technology Fluency Programme (ITFP) Test

docs.title: cGPA Requirement: The Academic Baseline
docs.text:
The most fundamental condition for graduation is that you must pass all compulsory courses and maintain a cumulative GPA (cGPA) of 1.67 or above.

Frequently skipping classes and failing to submit assignments can genuinely prevent you from graduating on time. Do not take this lightly! I know people who had to graduate a semester late simply because of poor class attendance.

docs.title: How is cGPA Calculated?
docs.text:
cGPA is the standard used to measure a student's academic performance. It is calculated by multiplying the credits of each course by the Grade Point earned, which gives the "Weighted Points." Finally, the total weighted points are divided by the total number of credits.

【Calculation Example】 Suppose you take 5 courses this semester, each worth 3 credits (15 credits in total):

Course Grade Grade Point Credits Weighted Points (Grade Point × Credits) Course A A 4.0 3 12.0 Course B B+ 3.3 3 9.9 Course C B 3.0 3 9.0 Course D C+ 2.3 3 6.9 Course E B- 2.7 3 8.1 Total - - 15 45.9
  • Total Weighted Points: 45.9
  • Total Credits: 15
  • Your cGPA: 45.9 / 15 = 3.06

docs.title: English Language Graduation Requirements (ELGR)
docs.text: All students must fulfill the language requirement by either passing the Password Test or achieving the required IELTS score. This requirement can be quite challenging, so it is highly recommended to allocate sufficient time to prepare for it.

docs.title: Comparison of the Two Assessment Methods
docs.text:
Assessment Attempt Requirements Graduation Score Threshold Fees & Resources Password Test(Easier, but has limited external recognition)
  • 4-Year Undergraduate Students: Take it twice in Year 1 and twice in Year 3–4 (4 times total).
  • Direct Entry / Senior-year Intake: Take it once in Year 3 and once in Year 4 (2 times total).
  • Most Majors: 6.5
  • Department of Chinese: 6.0
  • Department of English / Translation: 7.0
Arranged and funded by the university. IELTS(Globally recognized; can be taken anytime during your studies) All 4-year and Senior-year Intake students.
  • Most Majors: 6.5
  • Department of Chinese: 6.0
  • Department of English / Translation: 7.0
  • On-campus computer-based test fee is waived.
  • Off-campus test registration fees can be subsidized.
  • Official Preparation Resources: The university provides Online IELTS Resources for candidates. You can also make full use of the support services offered by the ELSS (English Language Support Service) to boost your English proficiency.

docs.title: Service Learning (SL)
docs.text:
Before graduating, you must enroll in and pass at least one Service Learning (SL) course. Unlike traditional lecture-based classes, these courses emphasize hands-on experience, where students independently plan and execute community service projects under the guidance of a supervisor.

  • How to Enroll: You register for it just like a regular course during the Course Registration period. The Registry's website provides a list of approved Service Learning courses available each term.
  • How to Pass: Complete the designated service activities according to the course guidelines and submit your reports on time.

Because Service Learning requires high autonomy and involves a relatively heavy workload and challenge, it is highly recommended to take it during Year 4.

docs.title: ILP Hours: Enriching Your Co-curricular Life
docs.text: The ILP (Integrated Learning Programme) comprises out-of-class holistic learning activities provided by the university. For every hour of participation, you earn 1 ILP point.

docs.title: The 6 ILP Categories
docs.text:
• CELD: Civic Education and Leadership Development
  • IED: Intellectual and Entrepreneurship Development
  • SEW: Social and Emotional Well-being
  • PFW: Physical Fitness and Well-being
  • AD: Aesthetic Development
  • RE: Residential Education

docs.title: Requirements for Freshmen vs. Senior-year Intakes
docs.text:
• 4-Year Undergraduate Freshmen:
    • Core Requirements: You must earn at least 5 points in each of the six categories (30 points total).
    • Free Electives: You must accumulate an additional 30 points from any category of your choice.
    • Total baseline requirement: 60 points.
  • Direct Entry / Senior-year Intake Students:
    • You only need to meet the core requirement of 3 points per category (18 points total). You are exempt from the 30 free elective points.

docs.title: Adjustments
docs.text:
• Absence from NSO: If you miss the New Student Orientation without a valid reason, your graduation requirement will increase by an extra 15 points of Free Electives.
  • Exchange Programmes: Successfully completing a university Exchange Programme grants you 7.5 points toward your Free Electives.

docs.title: How to Record Your Attendance and Points?
docs.text:
• In-person Activities: A QR code will be displayed at the beginning and end of the event. Make sure to scan it with your phone to check in and out.
  • Online Activities: Conducted via Zoom; the system will automatically log your attendance duration.
  • The Crucial Step: Within a week after the event ends, you will receive an Evaluation Form and a Reflection Report in your university email. Your ILP points will ONLY be officially credited to your account after you complete and submit both forms!

docs.title: How to Register for Activities & Earn ILP Points?
docs.text:
The university mainly distributes ILP activity information opportunities through three main channels:

Channel Description & Key Takeaways 1. Online Central Registration At the beginning of each semester, the university holds a centralized registration period. You will need to log into the system and select your preferred ILP activities, just like course registration. Note: Quotas are limited and offered on a first-come, first-served basis, so be sure to act fast! 2. Email Notifications Various university departments and organizations will send event invitations via email from time to time. Make sure to check your university inbox regularly! 3. Joining University Teams If you become an official team member and maintain an attendance rate of 80% or above, you can earn a substantial amount of ILP points directly:
  • Sports Teams: Awarded 12 PFW points directly (Physical Fitness and Well-being).
  • Cultural Teams: Awarded 12 AD points directly (Aesthetic Development).

docs.title: Information Technology Fluency Programme (ITFP)
docs.text:
Before graduation, you must pass the online ITFP test provided by the university.

  • Test Content: Covers basic computer operations and practical general knowledge of information literacy.
  • Test Link: Access the online ITFP Platform.

💡 A word from a senior: This test is a simple pass/fail assessment and is not difficult at all. Since you can take it at any point during your four years, I highly recommend getting it out of the way during your freshman year so you don't find yourself rushing to do it right before graduation.

Wishing you all a wonderful, fulfilling, and exciting four years at university. Graduate on time, and don't follow in my footsteps!

Author: Daniel, the Super-Senior

docs.title: 該不該住校？ Should you apply for studnet hostel?
docs.text: The application process for Lingnan University student hostels officially begins in early August. When you register via the Online Report System, you will be asked whether you wish to apply for a student hostel. This decision will define your daily life for the next three months. To help you make an informed choice, here is a breakdown of what you can expect.

docs.title: The Hostel Life Experience
docs.text:
A hostel is more than just a place to sleep; it is a vital part of your university experience and a catalyst for personal growth.

While your commuting peers are battling morning subway crowds and waking up at 7:00 AM to make an 8:00 AM class, you can sleep in and reach your lecture hall in a few minutes’ walk. During exam season, you won't have to fight for a seat in the library—your room becomes your private, convenient study sanctuary.

You will be living in close quarters 24/7. Whether it’s late-night study sessions, ordering midnight takeout, or sharing life’s ups and downs, these experiences often lead to lifelong friendships. You will never feel isolated, with constant social opportunities like orientation events, inter-hall competitions, floor gatherings, and annual hall banquets.

This is also your first step into adulthood. Without the constant oversight of family, you have the autonomy to manage your own schedule, from late-night projects to hanging out with friends.

docs.title: The Costs (And Hidden Challenges)
docs.text:
Before submitting your application, you must honestly evaluate whether you are prepared for the challenges of hostel living.

  1. Financial Commitment Living on campus is a significant investment. Below are the fees for the 2025-2026 academic year:
Location Room Charge Hall A - F Double Room $$7,875 ／ semester Hall G - H, WHC, WJY Double Room $8,700 ／ semester Hall G - H, WHC, WJY Triple Room $6,430 ／ semester

Each semester lasts approximately three months. Air conditioning fees are split among roommates. While internet and basic electricity are included, you will need to budget for daily essentials like laundry detergent, cleaning supplies, and toiletries.

The Hidden Challenges

  • The "Roommate Lottery": You cannot choose your roommates. Differences in lifestyle, sleeping habits, or study routines can easily lead to conflict.
  • Loss of Privacy: Hostel life is inherently communal. True solitude and total quiet are rare luxuries.
  • Increased Responsibility: There is no one to do your laundry or tidy your room. You must manage your own chores and daily maintenance.
  • The End-of-Term "Move-out": At the end of semester two, you are required to pack up all your belongings and move out, which can be logistically challenging.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Apply if: You crave independence, want to build deep social connections, and are excited to embrace the dynamic culture of hall life. Consider Commuting if: You place a high premium on personal privacy and quiet, or if you need to prioritize financial stability for your family. There is no shame in choosing to commute; it is often the most practical and mature decision depending on your personal circumstances.

By: Daniel

docs.title: 羅幼羚的傳奇 The Legend of Luo Youling
docs.text:
This story is entirely fictional. Luo Youling is not based on any real person.

Luo Youling: the heaviest name in the annals of this university. Had it not been for her, this institution might have long since eroded into dust from sheer, stagnant tranquility. Every blade of grass on this campus has borne witness to her Oedipal crusade.

The legend began in her first year. The administration repurposed a patch of sunny lawn into classrooms, citing a shortage of space. Luo launched her first-ever protest, publishing a 2,000-word manifesto of blood and tears on social media, lamenting that "the soul has nowhere to rest." In the end, she garnered two likes—one from her own burner account, and the other from a friend who hit the button by mistake.

In her second year, she initiated a series of campaigns that shook the administration to its core:

  • She vehemently protested the library’s use of "Ming" (Sim-Sun) font on signage, arguing that its lack of aesthetic design stifled students' creativity and freedom of thought. She demanded a complete switch to a serif typeface to uphold the university's humanistic integrity.
  • She accused the school of setting the hot water temperature in the teaching building’s water dispensers at only 85°C, rather than the “golden temperature” of 92°C—which is ideal for brewing coffee—and strongly criticized the administration for effectively depriving students of their quality of life and refined tastes by lowering the hot water temperature.
  • She attacked the university calendar for marking the "Exam Period" in red, asserting that such an intimidating color induced collective depression among students and demanding it be changed to a shade of light blue, symbolizing peace.

Her vision was a campus devoid of oppression, filled with aesthetics and justice. Her fighting spirit attracted as many as five "opponents" who joined her to form a massive organization called the "Campus Reform Concern Group," officially commencing a two-year Cold War with the administration office.

By her third year, Luo decided the group had reached "zero hour." That evening, four members gathered beside the administration building. Luo insisted on shouting at maximum volume, believing it to be a challenge to the systemic red line. When a security guard approached, she felt no shame; instead, a flicker of excitement flashed in her eyes. "Hello students, please keep your protest quiet. Don't disturb the dormitories," the guard gently reminded them.

She whispered to her members: "See? They’re panicking. They don't dare address our demands directly, so they send a pawn to engage in 'psychological warfare,' trying to break our resolve by citing 'noise disturbance.'" To her, that request from the guard was a sign that the highest levels of the administration were feeling unprecedented terror, even resorting to "dormitory public opinion" to suppress her. She viewed that minor warning as a historic victory for the group.

On the eve of graduation, she stood on the podium to recruit freshmen, her tone filled with a tragic hero’s arrogance. "I have led this university through its four darkest years," she told them. "Though the systems remain rigid, that only proves how formidable the enemy we face truly is—this 'utter lack of change' is the very proof of my existence."

Without her four years of struggle, this university would not be what it is today. Every institutional flaw is a "lesson" she has left for posterity. In her farewell speech, she framed these four years of futility as an "awakening movement." Even as she graduated to find the campus unchanged, she gazed at the gates that had never shifted, thinking to herself: "Thank goodness for me—it is precisely because of my presence that this mediocre school has preserved a flicker of resistance."

By: Daniel

docs.title: 不要成為一把瑞士軍刀 Don't Be a Swiss Army Knife
docs.text:
After uploading my resume to JobDB, I had three or four headhunting agencies reaching out within an hour, inviting me to apply for internship roles at top-tier firms. It sounds like an enviable position: I seemed to be the kind of candidate whose competitiveness makes employers come knocking. Yet, after submitting over 70 applications and going through 10 interviews, the result was consistently the same—I couldn’t land a single offer.

The problem? My resume had too many highlights.

If you look at the items on my resume individually, each one is quite impressive:

  • 2021 Census Enumerator: Coordinated resource allocation and administrative logistics for a team of 150 under high-pressure conditions.
  • Hospital Authority Administrative Assistant: Managed financial records and welfare applications for thousands of patients over four months, while implementing process automation using VBA and PowerBI.
  • Insurance Sales Associate: Worked on the front lines, generating over HK$200,000 in personal sales.
  • University Student Organization Officer: Spent 10 months managing press releases and internal administrative operations.
  • Technical Skills: Proficient in M language and VBA, with a solid foundation in R and SQL data analysis.

The contradiction lies in the fact that all these experiences were crammed onto a single resume.

In every interview, the interviewer would ask, 'What do you want to do after graduation?' No matter how I answered, it always sounded like a lie. If I said I wanted to be a professional financial advisor, they would question my low sales figures and assume I was too distracted by club activities to be fully committed. If I shifted gears and said I wanted to be a business data analyst, they would criticize my lack of technical depth and feel that my experience in public sectors made me ill-equipped for the fast-paced, high-flexibility rhythm of the private sector.

Many companies are looking for interns who are 'razor-sharp blades'—specialists in a specific domain. I, however, had turned myself into a 'Swiss Army knife.' While I could do a bit of everything, I appeared mediocre in everything. This is my dilemma: when you build yourself into a jack-of-all-trades, you become the most difficult risk to define in the eyes of the market.

Take it from me: if you are a freshman, you don’t need to rush to fill every gap on your resume with internships and competitions. Take the time to explore your true calling first, then commit to digging deep into that field. Those blindly stacked resume highlights might, in the eyes of a headhunter, be nothing more than a string of soulless keywords.

By:Daniel

docs.title: 如何更有效地學習 How to study more effectively
docs.text:
Is this person you? Rote memorizing key terms, skimming the powerpoints. But cannot remember what it is? Cannot answer deeper level of questions?

Here is the cue:

When I was in secondary school, I was taught that I should rote memorize every term or do as many past papers as I could. However, the reality is totally different! When I look at Justin Sung, a YouTuber who is famous for his educational tips and more, retention literally just went up.

The key mechanism is to let your brain struggle.

  1. Explain concepts in Bloom's revised taxonomy at least at level 3 instead of starting from the bottom

docs.title: 挑燈夜戰者的悲歌 A Tip for Pulling All-Nighters
docs.text:
The sofas in the Learning Commons (LYH 208)—they are truly not meant for human rest. Believe me, this is a 'hard-learned' lesson from someone who has been there. It was late at night before an exam, and when I finally finished studying the last chapter and looked at my phone, I was shocked to see it was already 2:00 AM. At that moment, curled up on that rock-hard sofa, I felt no sense of satisfaction. What we call 'pulling an all-nighter' is often just a final, desperate struggle resulting from poor time management.

University offers students unprecedented freedom, but the price of that freedom is the responsibility to manage your own time. If you don't want to spend your exam season sleeping on the hard chairs of the library, please be sure to learn the following principles of time management.

docs.title: Define Your 'Priorities'
docs.text:
You must determine the order of priority among your academic research, extracurricular organizations, career exploration, and personal relationships. Academics are only one part of university life. That semester, I received an invitation to a banking industry event that offered direct insight into industry trends and culture. The cost was missing two days of classes. I thought to myself, 'It’s only two days of progress; it shouldn't be hard to catch up.' The result was that I ended up having to spend even more time catching up later. You need to learn to assess: Do I have more important things to do? A clear goal can help you filter out ineffective social commitments and activities, allowing you to invest your energy in the most critical tasks.

Goals also need to be time-bound and measurable. You might try inputting all your assignment deadlines and exam dates into your calendar during the first week of the semester, allowing the pressure of 'deadlines' to transform into the motivation to take action rather than procrastinate.

docs.title: Create Time for 'Deep Work'
docs.text:
You must carve out time for 'deep work,' focusing on only one goal at a time. Multitasking significantly reduces your productivity. I once made a classic mistake: trying to handle group projects while preparing for midterms. Both deadlines were within the same week. When I finally sat down to open my textbook, my phone started buzzing. My group members were having a heated debate about the report's arguments in the chat, and I thought, 'Just replying once shouldn't matter.' That one reply turned into half an hour of arguing. By the time I put my phone down and returned to my books, my train of thought was long broken, my mind was blank, and I had to start reading all over again.

The result: I spent three hours and didn't even finish a single chapter. That sense of disconnect—where I was 'studying,' but my brain was still on my phone—was more exhausting than anything else. Remember to set a 'no-distraction time' for yourself. Put your phone on 'Do Not Disturb,' disconnect from social media, and focus entirely on the single most important task. Leave trivial matters like replying to messages, organizing emails, or simple data collection for a specific, dedicated block of time.

However, be careful not to pack your calendar entirely with work. You need to leave room for rest and unexpected situations.

docs.title: Dynamic Adjustment
docs.text:
Time management is a dynamic collaboration; plans must adapt to change. Take a few dozen minutes every week to review your progress and adjust your calendar for the coming week. If you find that the importance of a certain goal has decreased, or that your time allocation was too idealistic, don't hesitate to make changes. Re-evaluate your own work efficiency and set goals that are within your capabilities.

Effective time management isn't about doing more; it’s about freeing up time to 'experience' the beauty of university—to exercise, to read, to engage in deep conversations with like-minded friends—rather than wasting your life away on a library sofa.

I hope not to see you at the library in the middle of the night.

docs.title: 輪椅人士之入lingu建議 Advice for Wheelchair Users in Lingnan
docs.text:
Lingnan University (Lingu) is a relatively wheelchair-friendly university. If the SEN (Special Educational Needs) team has not contacted you yet, please proactively reach out to them by sending an email to sen@ln.edu.hk, calling 2616 7119 / 2616 7308, or filling out the online form at https://www.ln.edu.hk/osa/sen (scroll down to the bottom of the page).

If you plan to live in student housing, Hall G and Hall H feature single wheelchair-accessible rooms. The restrooms inside are spacious and equipped with barrier-free facilities such as grab bars and shower stools, with all heights tailored for wheelchair users. Caregivers are also permitted to live in with you (the author was actually the first case). If you need this, let the SEN team know as soon as possible, and the Hostel Team will follow up.

Orientation and Exam Accommodations Once your SEN registration is complete, staff will be assigned to assist you on New Student Orientation (NSO) day, so there is no need to worry. A major benefit of SEN services is special exam arrangements. As long as you submit the relevant reports and follow DSE-style accommodations, the university is generally very accommodating and lenient without making things difficult for you. Feel free to make requests without pressure. Exams typically do not take place in the large Chan Sui Kau Gymnasium, but rather in the adjacent table tennis or squash courts.

Activities and ILP PFW Requirements The SEN team organizes various activities specifically for SEN students. If you worry about feeling pressured in other events, these can be great opportunities to make friends. Lingnan University does not exempt wheelchair users from the ILP PFW (Physical Education and Well-being) requirement (first-year entry students must earn at least 5 points). Since most activities are sports-oriented and hard for wheelchair users to participate in, lectures or SEN events offering ILP PFW points are in very high demand.

Campus Facilities and Environment Lingnan's campus is relatively small; except for a few gardens and areas past the third pavilion, most places are accessible. However, due to ongoing construction of a new building, traveling from the Leung Kau Kui Building (LKK) toward the main entrance requires a detour near the canteen to find a ramp. It is recommended to plan extra travel time.

Campus Access and Restrooms

Entrances: The main entrance has no barrier-free access—only stairs—and the stair lift is frequently out of order. Waiting for it takes longer than simply detouring to a side gate. It is recommended to enter via the footbridge or the North Gate (near Chelsea Heights or Fu Tai Estate).

Restrooms: The most convenient restrooms are inside the residence halls, considering it takes a 10 to 15-minute wheelchair ride from PST or S.H. Ho Hall (SEK). If you need to use a restroom on campus, two larger options are recommended: the one at Learning Commons on the 2nd floor of Lau Chung Him Building (LYH), and the one outside the elevators on the ground floor of SEK. Other restrooms are usable, but tend to be cramped and less clean.

Transportation Transportation options are basically the same as for everyone else. If you take bus K51 or K51A, getting off at the stop after "Lingnan University"—closer to Fu Tai Estate or the North Gate—makes it much easier to enter the campus, as the main entrance is impassable and the North Gate is far more convenient.

Social Life Many wheelchair users worry about failing to make friends in university, but there is no need to overthink it at Lingnan. Everyone is very friendly, willing to greet you and hold doors open. Naturally, you still need to take the initiative to talk to people to build relationships. The author has experience joining a student society ("sheung chong"). Whether you choose to join a society or participate in O-day/O-camp depends entirely on your own physical condition. If interested, you can check with the societies beforehand or attend the Affiliated Societies Night on September 3 to look around without fear.

Author: Takumi Fujiwara in a Purple Electric Wheelchair (AI-adapted)
